analytic.title: A Flexible Service Reservation Scheme for Real-Time SOA

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper addresses the problem of resource reservation for applications built using the real-time serviceoriented architecture (RT-SOA) paradigm. Real-time services can choose some time inside of a large interval for execution reservation. This property gives services more chance to be accepted by the schedulability admission control. However, the traditional way of advance reservation on fixed schedules does not take advantage of this flexibility. In this paper, a reorganization algorithm is presented to relocate existing reservations if necessary to accommodate new requests that have a less flexibility. Simulation results show that reorganization can enhance the acceptance ratio of real-time requests in almost all situations. When jobs have flexible real-time requirements, acceptance ratio can be greatly enhanced.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Service-oriented architecture (SOA) is a way of using existing services to compose distributed workflows. As a comparative novel architecture, it brings software developers with the characteristics of loosely coupling, implementation neutrality, flexible configurability, persistence and distributed computing [1]. SOA brings about many research questions in guaranteeing the QoS of composite workflow. In some mission-critical fields like banking, industrial automation and online transaction, beside the common QoS requirements, there are also some real-time requirements, such as an end-toend response time requirement that must not be violated. We therefore study the problem of how to achieve predictability in composing workflows in these time-critical RT-SOA applications.

In our work on RT-Llama [2], we address this problem by using advance reservation on service hosts. Intermediate start time and deadline are assigned to each service in the workflow to guarantee that the overall end-to-end deadline is met. In RT-Llama, we implement a global resource manager and several local resource managers. The global resource manager is a central middleware component which is in charge of composing workflows and making reservations in all participating service hosts. The local resource managers on service hosts are used to make reservations and sched-ule service execution locally. Executors in local resource managers use the earliest deadline first (EDF) algorithm to schedule services.

RT-Llama uses an hTBTree data structure [3] to make a capacity reservation on intervals, not specific time slots, in local resource managers. However, once reserved, reservations are bound to the sub-intervals selected. In this paper, we propose another data structure called job tree to store the job reservation information and design a reorganization algorithm. The reorganization algorithm can relocate existing reservations to accommodate new service requests. The algorithm and the data structure are implemented based on the RT-Llama framework and hTBTree. Experimental results with and without reorganization are compared in the paper.

The contribution of this work is the new admission algorithm and efficient data structure designed for re-scheduling of real-time services with execution interval constraints. Since service requests may arrive at random orders (in terms of their deadlines), latter requests may find their execution intervals have been taken by earlier requests. By moving earlier requests to make room for latter requests, a system can admit more real-time services. This is very useful for RT-SOA.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. II defines the real-time service model and shows the hTBTree data structure. It also gives a simple motivation example for reorganization. Sec. III presents the reorganization algorithms and introduces job tree, the new data structure we use to store job reservation information. The performance of reorganization is shown in Sec. IV. Sec. V compares our work with previous works on advance reservation. Finally we conclude our work in Sec. VI. end-to-end deadline and corresponding service process flow. From these, intermediate start times and deadlines of services in the flow can be decided. Details on the mechanism of deciding what the intermediate deadlines and start times are can be found in [2]. Note that the start time of the first job(s) is equal to the task start time and the deadline of the last job(s) is equal to the task absolute deadline. The system needs to check the schedulability of each real-time task. However, if all of the component jobs of a task are schedulable, then a task is also schedulable. So we can simplify the problem of schedulability check for a task to schedulability check for all individual jobs. For the rest of paper, we only consider the schedulability for individual jobs.

Specifically in the model, any job request Req i is defined by an individual start times s i , an individual deadline d i and a worst-case execution time wcet i . Since the system does not know about future task requests, every time a real-time job arrives, the system tries to reserve it. Jobs are preemptable in the system. So in the model, when a job is successfully reserved, the reservation can include allocations from different time intervals. We call each of the reservation allocations a sub-interval. Intervals and subintervals are all defined by their lower ends and upper ends and are expressed in the form of [lower end, upper end]. So each job reservation Job i could consist of j allocations: alloc i,j = (interval i,j , time i,j ), j = 0, 1, 2.... interval i,j is the interval for the corresponding allocation and time i,j is the reserved time in the interval. There should be no overlap among the allocations of each job: ∀alloc(i, j 1 ), alloc(i, j 2 ) of Job i , interval i,j1 interval i,j2 = ∅. We can define a job reservation as a combination of Req i and its allocations:
div.formula: Job i = ([s i , d i ], wcet i , {alloc i,j , j = 0, 1, 2....})

div.head: B. The hTBTree Design
div.p: In RT-Llama, the schedulability test for job reservations is conducted using a data structure called hTBTree [3]. On every host, there is a resource manager which uses an hTBTree to record the idle time in future intervals. HTBTree can also be used to look up estimated utilization at a future time.

Derived from Temporal Bin Tree [4], hTBTree is a binary tree in which resource availability over a certain period of time is recorded. In this paper, the resource is the CPU capacity. The root node of the tree is used to store the capacity availability over the complete time interval. Each node in the tree covers one half of its parent's interval and records the spare time left in that interval. One example of an empty hTBTree is shown in Fig. 1(a). Each tree node is shown with (interval : idle) pair in the graph. In this example the interval of the root is from 0 to 8. Each of the leaf nodes is used to express resource availability of 1 time unit; thus the granularity of the tree is 1. For the rest of this paper, since each hTBTree node has a unique interval, we'll use the interval field to identify the tree node for simplicity.

Any job reservation on an hTBTree is made on the Minimum Coverage Set (MCS) of the node intervals in the tree. MCS is defined as the minimum set of intervals in the tree that can cover the job interval. For example in Fig. 1(a), if there is a job Req 1 = ( [1,5], 2), the MCS of interval [1,5] is [1,2], [2,4], [4,5]. These 3 intervals are shown as red boxes in Fig. 1

div.head: (b).
div.p: There are three basic operations for hTBTree [3].

• Allocation: For allocations on an hTBTree, the set of {interval i,j |j = 0, 1...} is just the MCS of interval i . An allocation alloc i,j on an hTBTree would not only reduce the idle field of the hTBTree node containing interval i,j by time i,j , but also reduce the idle field of all ancestor nodes on the path from interval i,j to the root by time i,j . This ensures the idle consistency in the tree. There are different policies on selecting allocation intervals from the MCS for reservation [3].

In this paper we use the earliest fit policy which tries to make reservations from the earliest intervals. Fig. 1(b) shows the hTBTree after the reservation of Req 1 using the earliest fit policy. • Look up: Since nodes only notify ancestors about allocations in the interval, if we want to look up how much spare time an interval interval i,j still has, we need to see both the idle in interval i,j and idles in all interval i,j 's ancestors. The spare space equals to the minimum of idles of interval i,j and all its ancestors. For instance, in the example of Fig. 1(b) after the reservation of Req 1 , the time units we can still reserve inside interval [2,4] would be the minimum of idles in time intervals [2,4], [0, 4], [0,8]; in this case it is 1. • Deletion: In case a task is terminated, its reservations can be deleted. Information about reservations are recorded in a data structure called job tree which will be introduced in Section. III-D. The operation of deletion is similar to allocation except that it needs to release those reserved time units. More details on hTBTree can be found in [3].

div.head: III. REORGANIZATION
div.p: By making reservation in MCS, hTBTree achieves a better flexibility than the original TBTree [3]. However, allocations in hTBTree are still bound to fixed intervals. This may cause latter reservation requests to be rejected if they must use an earlier, but already allocated, time interval. A motivating example is shown in Fig. 1(c). This figure shows an hTBTree after 5 job requests. Then a reservation request Req 6 = ( [1,4], 2) arrives. Since interval [1,2] can accommodate no more reservation and [2,4] can accommodate only 1 more time unit due to the Req 1 reservation, Req 6 would be rejected. However, if we allocate reservation for Req 1 in a different way, by allocating 1 time unit in [1, 2] and 1 time unit in [4,5], there will be enough space in [2,4] to accommodate Req 6 . The result after reserving Req 6 is shown in Fig. 1(d). Since the system does not have knowledge on future jobs, it is impossible to decide which way of making reservation for Req 1 is better before the arrival of Req 6 . So a reorganization algorithm which relocates existing reservations to make room for future reservations is needed to make the allocations more flexible.

div.head: A. Triggering Reorganization
div.p: For each job reservation, reorganization is triggered when a new job reservation cannot be reserved. Algorithm 1 shows when to trigger reorganization in hTBTree. In the algorithm, it tries to allocate wcet units of time units in time interval I. Line 3 identifies the MCS of interval I. Line 4 creates a status variable to see if there is still idle time from one of the MCS intervals. Then in lines 7-19, the algorithm tries to reserve wcet units of time in the MCS intervals. The resulting allocation list allocLst is also updated during the reservation. After that, in line 21, the algorithm checks if the reservation is complete. If there is still some time to be reserved, it begins reorganization on some admitted jobs. In line 24, the next partially overlapping admitted job interval is identified, then line 28 performs reorganization on this admitted job interval. We'll explain it in details in the next subsection. Suppose there are at most S sub-intervals for a reservation and the height of hTBTree is H. Checking idle for all m's ancestors takes O(H) time, so the worst case complexity of making reservation without reorganization is O(SH).

div.head: B. Relocation in Reorganization
div.p: The basic idea of reorganization is to relocate allocations of prior reservations in order to make room for new reservation requests. If prior reservations do not have overlap with the new request's time interval, they should not affect the new request directly. So we only consider the ones with overlaps.

In our algorithm, for a new request, it considers one overlapping admitted reservation at a time. We call the new request the requesting job and call existing reservations as admitted jobs. The reorganization moves allocations in some admitted jobs. As shown in Fig. 2, depending on the degree of overlap with the requesting job interval, we can divide the sub-intervals of an admitted job into three categories.

• If a sub-interval does not overlap with the requesting job interval, it belongs to Type N , the non-overlapping type; • If a sub-interval partially overlaps with the requesting job interval, it belongs to Type P , the partial-overlapping type; • If a sub-interval resides within the borders of the requesting job interval, it belongs to Type A, the alloverlapping type. for each hTBTree node m in mcs do 8:

available ← min(idles of m and its ancestors) hasIdle ← reorganization(I, J, need) 29: end while 30: return false To make room for a requesting job, allocations in admitted jobs can be moved out of type A intervals and into type N intervals. However, for type P , it requires more testing. Based on whether a type P can be used like a type A to move out allocations, or to receive allocations like a type N , we can further divide it into type P a and type P n . Algorithm 1 triggers reorganization only after a requesting job takes the remaining idle time from all of its sub-intervals but still does not have enough. Under this condition, a type P sub-interval cannot be a type P a and type P n at the same time. If a type P sub-interval has non-zero idle space, it means this sub-interval is not needed for reserving the requesting job.

And it would yield no extra room for the requesting job if allocations are moved out of it. On the other hand if a type P sub-interval has zero idle space, it means the sub-interval cannot accept more reservation. So we need to distinguish between zero and non-zero idle space type P intervals to decide whether a type P interval is of type P a or type P n .

We also need to decide how much time can be moved. For type A, it can move all its allocated units out; for type N , it can use its spare space to hold incoming allocations. For type P n , it's the same case as type N . However, for type P a , it's different from type A. The maximum useful amount for P a is limited by both the total allocation amount currently in the sub-interval and the length of intersection between requesting job interval and the move destination sub-interval because move amount greater than the intersection is not necessary. Also, the amount may depend on allocations in some other sub-intervals.

We can see this from the example in Fig. 3. The figure shows an hTBTree with 2 reservations. When the third request of ([1, 3], 2) arrives, since the idle of [0, 4] in the tree is 0, a reorganization is needed. It first considers Job 1 . The [0, 4] interval of alloc 1,1 is partially overlapping with job 3 and is fully occupied thus is of type P a , the [4,6] interval of alloc 1,2 is of type N . So it can move time units from alloc 1,1 to alloc 1,2 . The intersection between alloc 1,1 and Job 3 is 2 and time 1,1 is 2. So 2 time units can be moved from [0, 4] to [4,6]. However, although 2 time units are moved away, only 1 more unit can be accommodated for Job 3 , because Job 2 also has some allocations in interval [1,3]. So we need to try reserve requesting job again after relocating allocations in every admitted job, to test how many more time units can be reserved after moves.

div.head: C. Reorganization Algorithm
div.p: The detailed reorganization algorithm is shown in Algorithm 2. Lines 1-18 classify sub-intervals into the 4 different lists lstA, lstP a , lstP n , lstN that contain the 4 types of sub-intervals respectively. The amount of time that each sub-interval can move is also stored with sub-intervals. So elements in the lists have tuples of (interval, move amount). Lines 19 and 20 generate the lists for relocation source and destination. And line 21 calculates the total units that can be moved in a specific admitted job. The sum on this line is the sum of movable amount from the corresponding list, which can be calculated while constructing the lists. Note that the number may not be equal to the extra time units that can be reserved for the requesting job after moving the allocations. Lines 22 moves allocations from the sub-intervals in the list of move source to the sub-intervals in the list of move destination. Line 23 checks if the moved amount is non-zero. If so, the algorithm will return true to Algorithm 1 (Line 28), which will try to reserve the requesting job interval again to see how many more units are still needed.

The complexity of the reorganization operation can be analyzed as follows. Suppose the maximum number of subintervals in a job reservation is S and there are n jobs currently reserved in the system. Also suppose the time to look up how many time units we can still put into a subinterval is L. In the worst case, for a new job reservation, we need to go through all existing reservations in a system. For every existing reservation, we need to go through all its subintervals twice: the first time is for sub-interval remaining capacity look-up and categorization,the second time is for deciding how we do the move. So the complexity for this part is O(2SL). For every existing reservations, we also need to try reserving in the requesting job interval which need to look up the remaining capacity for each of the sub-intervals of requesting job and the complexity for this part is O(SL). So the combined complexity is O(3SL) for one job reservation and thus O(nSL) for all reservations in the system.

div.head: In hTBTree, the length of MCS is at most 2(H -1)(at most 2 sub-intervals in each layer of hTBTree except the root layer). So S = O(2(H -1)) and L = O(H). So the combined complexity of both reservation and reorganization is O(2(H -1)H + 6n(H -1)H), namely O(nH 2
div.p: ). If the leaf node of hTBTree can express 10 ms of time span, an hTBTree of 30 layers can cover about 116 days. In fact, real-time service reservation requests whose execution times are usually hundreds of milliseconds to seconds will not need advance reservations of that far. So we can assume the height of hTBTree would not exceed 30. Indeed, H can be treated as a constant, and the complexity of the overall reservation and reorganization operation for one request is O(n).

div.head: D. Job Tree
div.p: Line 24 of Algorithm 1 wants to find the next partially overlapping admitted job intervals for reorganization. In our implementation, we design a job tree which is based on the red-black tree to store existing reservations. The job tree is indexed by the upper end d of job intervals in ascending order. A basic node inside our job tree is shown in Fig. 4. The node also has the fields of min and max; min is the smallest lower end of intervals in the subtree, while max is the largest upper end of intervals in the subtree. There are four operations defined for a job tree.
• Single insertion: the operation of insertion a node into the job tree is similar to that operation in red-black tree.

The insertion starts from the root. Depending on the result of comparing the upper end d of requesting job and that of admitted jobs, the tree decides which branch the requesting job node should go into. The insertion operation also changes the min and max fields of nodes along the path. After inserting the requesting job into the tree as a leaf node, the tree also needs to do O(log n ) fix-up operations to keep the whole tree balanced as in red-black tree. • Single deletion: If a job reservation is canceled, we need to delete the corresponding job tree node. Similar to single insertion, we start from the root searching for the node. After it is found, we delete it, change the min, max fields of ancestor nodes if needed, and conduct the red-black tree node deletion fix-up algorithm whose complexity is also O(log n ). • Multiple deletion: When some jobs' deadlines have passed, we no longer need to keep the jobs in the job tree. So we also want to delete outdated jobs. To maintain the complexity of deletion to O(log n ), this operation does not delete all outdated jobs. Instead, it searches for the first outdated job node whose complete left branch is outdated (by comparing max of its left child with the current time), deletes the job node and its whole left branch, and replaces it with its right child. After that, O(log n ) fix-up operations which are similar to that of single deletion is needed to maintain the balance of the tree. • Overlapping intervals searching: We need to search for partially overlapping intervals. In the worst case, it would be to traverse the whole job tree. To reduce the time used for searching, we use the min and max fields to help trim down some branches of intervals. For a job tree node along the searching, if a) its min field is greater than the upper end d of requesting job interval I, or b) its max field is smaller than the lower end s of requesting job interval I, or c) [min, max] ∈ I, all these cases indicate there is no partially overlapping target intervals inside the subtree. So we can skip searching in these branches to improve the search speed.

The process of searching the example job tree in Fig. 1(c) and Fig. 1(d) is given below. Fig. 5(a) shows how 5 prior reservations are stored in job tree. The colors of node borders indicate the colors of nodes as of a red-black tree property. Before a reorganization, the algorithm tries to reserve the requesting job but can only reserve one unit in sub-interval [2,4]. So we need to do reorganization to make room for the other unit. If we are using pre-order traversing in job tree for search, we first go into the root node, finding there are two type A sub-intervals:[1, 2], [2,4] and one type N subinterval: [4,5]. So according to Algorithm 2, we move one time unit from [1,2] to [4,5]. Then, we try reserve again and find that we can reserve 1 unit into [1,2]. Thus, all the needed time can now be reserved and reorganization returns success. Actually the interval of job request 6 is [1,4] which has no overlapping with interval [4,8] of the right child of the root node. Even if we need to continue searching, there is no need to search in the subtree. The resulting job tree is shown in Fig. 5(b).
(a) the job tree before reorganization for request6.

(b) the job tree after reorganization for request6. • Task Ratio(tr): tr = 1 n Σ n i=1 wceti di-si . It reflects how demanding real-time reservations are. The larger the task ratio, the less flexibility the jobs have for reorganization.

• Out-of-Order Ratio(ooo): Given a sorted list of execution requests, the simulation randomly selects one of the next r requests (or the remaining requests if the number of requests is less than r). This is to simulate out of order request arrivals. We define ooo = log 10 r. ooo = 0 means there is no occurrence of out-of-order request.

We compare the effectiveness of reorganization by the percentage of the acceptance ratio improvement over the original acceptance ratio. In other words, reorganization effect is equal to the number of reorganization success divided by the number of success reservation without reorganization.

In the simulation, we test traffic density from 0.2 to 1.4, task ratio from 0.1 to 0.9 and out-of-order ratio from 0 to 3. The request arrival pattern is modeled as a Poisson process. In our simulation, the average inter-arrival time of jobs is 248 time units. We first build a sorted list of requests with inter-arrival times defined by the Poisson process. The actual ordering of reservation requests is selected based on the out-of-order ratio. For each combination of parameters, we generate a wcet and use the same wcet for 1000 jobs. So all reservations in a single run are also of identical interval length due to the same task ratio. We store reservations on an hTBTree of height 18 whose leaf nodes are all 1 unit time interval. For every combination of parameters, we run for ten times, collect results and calculate the average reorganization effect of the ten runs.
We now discuss 3 out-of-order ratio conditions:

• ooo = 0: All requests come in order. Because all requests have identical intervals and because we use the Earliest-Fit policy which tries to reserve allocations as early as possible, requests arriving in-order also means requests are reserved according to their deadlines. So reorganization cannot improve the effectiveness. Experiments show 0 reorganization effects for all ooo = 0 cases. • ooo = 1: The next request is randomly selected from one of next 10 sorted requests. An intuitive expectation is that a higher traffic density and a lower task ratio tend to have a better reorganization effect. However the result (Fig. 6) shows that when both traffic density and task ratio are relative low, the reorganization effect increases as task ratio grows higher. This is because the original fixed reservation of hTBTree can also take advantage from this condition. Fig. 7 shows the numbers of accepted requests with and without reorganization when task ratio is 0.1. We can see from Fig. 7 when the traffic density is not too high, reorganization helps to make nearly all of the requests accepted. However due to the normal reservation part of hTBTree already did a good job, the improvement of reorganization effect is still limited. In this case, since only unsuccessful reservations trigger the reorganization operation, the complexity caused by reorganization is also limited. The best reorganization effect is achieved when traffic is heavy, i.e. when traffic density is 1.4. In that case, the reorganization effect can reach about 20% when tr = 0.1 and the average total accepted request number would reach 688.1 while the highest possible acceptance number is less than 1000 1.4 = 714.3.

• ooo = 3 : The next request is randomly selected from one of the sorted 1000 requests. Since there are a total of 1000 requests, all requests arrive in a totally random pattern. The reorganization effect is shown in Fig. 8. It shows a similar trend as Fig. 6 except the cases when traffic density is high and task ratio is low. When traffic density is 1.4 and task ratio is 0.1, the average total accepted number is 664 which is also a very high compared with the highest possible acceptance number of 714. From the observation, we see reorganization can achieve a higher number of acceptance when task ratio is lower and can improve 5 to 15 percent of the original acceptance ratio with a higher task ratio. When task ratio becomes higher than 0.8, reorganization would not be that effective.

div.head: V. RELATED WORK
div.p: Many projects have been studied on advance reservation. While most use fixed advance reservation with static job start time and end time, some have tried to make advance reservations more flexible. Techniques including using start time shifting, processor remapping, malleable reservations of changing rectangular shape for rescheduling when a new reservation request arrives [5][6]. However, no project considers preemptable reservations that might be divisible. Also, the rescheduling operations result in a high fragmentation of time in their reservations. In [7], authors discuss about elastic scheduling. Their reservations are made of smaller allocations and can be reallocated to accommodate new requests which are similar to our reservations. But their allocations are all based on basic time slots. Also, their models assume earlier requests to have a higher priority while our algorithm only concentrates on the real-time property that as long as earlier reserved requests' deadlines are met, we consider all earlier reservations for reorganization.

In the field of Service-Oriented Computing, there are many works addressing the QoS issues but not many have addressed the issue of predictability. [8] presents a schedulability check algorithm to help guarantee real-time computing. One merit of the algorithm is that it does not assign specific allocations to reservations. However in the worst case they still need to check all existing reservations and their algorithm of O(n 2 ) is slow for on-line checking when there are a lot of reservations in the system. [9] tries to group overlapping parts of reservations and used a probabilistic model to express the overlapping parts. However, in their study, all reservations of the same interval just have the same probability to be executed which is not always true.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we present an approach for reorganizing reserved service process schedules in RT-SOA. The study aims at enhancing the acceptance ratio in the admission control of real-time service processes. We have designed a job tree data structure, which is a variation of the red-black tree, to store jobs and allocation information for efficient insertion and deletion operations. The effectiveness of reorganization algorithm has been studied based on reservations under different workloads and different job arrival patterns. Simulation results show that reorganization works well for task ratio lower than 0.8 and medium traffic density. With a high traffic density, the acceptance ratio can get an improvement as high as 20% compared with a fixed reservation. This suggests reorganization can be effective in heavily-loaded real-time SOA systems.
